messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The crash happened on a Tuesday afternoon, just after three o’clock. Ravi was driving home from the community center where he worked as a program coordinator, his mind half-occupied with the next month’s food distribution schedule. He never saw the pickup truck that ran the red light. He only remembered the sound—a shattering, metallic roar that seemed to come from inside his own skull—and then the feeling of his car spinning, the seatbelt cutting into his chest, and his hands gripping the steering wheel with a strength he didn’t know he had. When the world finally stopped moving, he was facing oncoming traffic, and the air smelled of gasoline and hot rubber. He was not physically injured, but something in him had been torn loose. For weeks afterward, every time he closed his eyes, he saw the grille of that truck growing larger, and the terror he had felt in that moment returned as fresh as if he were still sitting in the wreckage. The images came to him unbidden, mostly pictures—the shattered windshield, the dashboard twisted sideways—and when they arrived, he felt himself back inside the car, his heart hammering, his breath short, his body tensed for an impact that had already happened.

Ravi had always been a calm man, the sort of person colleagues described as unflappable. That changed. He began to notice that certain textures—the rough fabric of his car’s seat cover, the stiff denim of his jeans—would suddenly pull him back into the crash, as if his skin remembered the way the seatbelt had pressed against him. He learned to avoid those textures, choosing softer clothes, sitting only on smooth surfaces, but the world was full of triggers he could not anticipate. A car accident on the evening news, or a colleague mentioning a fender bender, would drop him straight into a reliving episode, his hands shaking, his vision tunneling. He started to dread conversations, steering them away from any topic that might lead to talk of accidents. At work, he found himself excusing himself from meetings when someone began describing a minor collision, his pulse already racing before he had consciously registered the topic.

The worst moments came without warning. A sudden loud sound—a car backfiring, a door slamming, a dropped tray in the cafeteria—would send a jolt through him, and he would be on his feet, scanning for danger, his body braced for a blow. He hated this hypervigilance, the way it made him feel like a stranger in his own skin. And yet, the more he scanned, the more he noticed movement at the edges of his vision, and each unexpected motion—a child darting across a parking lot, a cyclist weaving through traffic—triggered the same startle response, the same flood of fear. These moments, in turn, seemed to summon the memories. A sudden jerk of his head toward a sound, and he would be back in the car, watching the truck approach, his hands frozen on the wheel. It was a loop he could not break: the memories made him watchful, and the watching brought the memories back.

By the time he sought help, six months after the crash, Ravi had stopped driving entirely. He took the bus to work, but even that felt precarious; every sudden brake, every horn blast, sent him into a spiral. He had begun to avoid going out at all. His wife, Meera, had grown frustrated with his silences, with the way he would flinch when she touched his shoulder from behind. He could not explain it to her—how the texture of her hand on his shirt could, in a fraction of a second, become the pressure of the seatbelt, the smell of gasoline, the sound of metal tearing. What frightened him most was the feeling that the crash was still happening, that he was still in that spinning car, waiting for the world to stop. He came to therapy because he was tired of being afraid, and because he had started to wonder if he would ever feel safe again.
